texts: mixed: the rule fires and every part of the sentence is covered, but "salt-bloom blooms" collides with itself - the noun salt-bloom is broken down to its head "bloom", and the verb "blooms" lands on that same symbol, so each blooming event falls into the very class the substance is a kind of. Use a verb that is not the noun's own head: "When a spring tide fills the tide-pools, salt-bloom forms in the tide-pools." (your "grows" wording avoids it too).
good. the trigger is quantified over spring tides, the definite tide-pools are introduced once and reused in the result, and the growing is tied to the tide that caused it.
good. "crystalline crust" is fused as the kind while the colour "pale" stays a separate property - the right split - and nothing is asserted beyond what the sentence says.

bad: this reads as one particular dissolving that happened rather than a standing fact about salt-bloom, so it is recorded as a single event at full confidence instead of a rule that applies to any salt-bloom. Put it in the same conditional form as your other rules: "Whenever salt-bloom touches the seawater, that salt-bloom quickly dissolves into it."
